title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

infographic.key_insight: In RL with verifiable rewards, momentum can help if the EMA coefficient is set large enough to stay in a safe, non-overshooting regime; otherwise sampling noise can hide its benefit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM post-training, tuning momentum upward can yield measurable accuracy gains and should be treated as a practical hyperparameter rather than a default setting.
method: Analyze RLVR as a bandit problem with bias-corrected EMA momentum.
Prove that larger \u03b2 accelerates optimization when exact gradients are used and overshoot is avoided.
Show that under sampled gradients, shrinking learning rate alone can wash out the momentum gain, while jointly increasing \u03b2 preserves it.
infographic.evidence_signal: Bandit simulations and RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen2.5-32B validate the theory, with larger \u03b2_1 improving mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 percentage points on the larger model.
infographic.watch_item: The benefit depends on keeping \u03b7/(1-\u03b2) in a safe regime; too-small or poorly matched settings can obscure gains or cause overshoot.
infographic.paper_title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
authors: Weichen Lyu, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong, Long Xu, Shengjun Zhang, Yueqi Duan
abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.

infographic.key_insight: PhySGA frames 3D composition as an interactive physics-space agent task, combining planning, simulation, and feedback to assemble objects more reliably than static-prior methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is directly relevant to digital content creation and robot simulation because it improves physically plausible assembly for rigid, articulated, and deformable objects.
method: Assembly Agent plans global steps and performs coarse geometric/kinematic adjustments.
Critic Agent diagnoses simulator states using contact dynamics and provides fine-grained closed-loop corrections.
Action Routers execute semantic plans as physical simulator primitives, while a Self-Evolving Skill Library reuses successful trial-and-error experience.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive experiments in Isaac Sim showing improved relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality over existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on simulator fidelity and the quality of agent routing/skills, so transferring the approach to new scenes or simulators could require careful re-tuning.
infographic.paper_title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition

title: Modeling and Understanding Neural Weights of Humanoid Policies with Diffusion
authors: Huixuan Cheng, Bike Zhang, Shankar Sastry, Koushil Sreenath
abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/

infographic.key_insight: A latent diffusion model can generate functional humanoid control policies directly in weight space, and the learned weights appear to encode a shared kinematic prior across training paradigms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a new route for synthesizing deployable robot controllers and for interpreting which structural features of policy weights are tied to humanoid embodiment.
method: Train a linear autoencoder to compress actor-network parameters into a latent space.
Use a Diffusion Transformer to model and sample the latent weight distribution.
Decode sampled latents back into full control networks for deployment and analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was trained on RL-derived networks from the Unitree G1 and produced real-world policies capable of walking, dancing, and spin kicks, while analysis revealed a consistent first-layer structural pattern linked to kinematic priors under both RL and IL.
infographic.watch_item: Generative weight-space models may produce deployable controllers only if the training set is sufficiently diverse and the decoded weights preserve safety and stability under real-world robot dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Modeling and Understanding Neural Weights of Humanoid Policies with Diffusion

title: Revisiting Simple Baselines for Relational Deep Learning
authors: Viet The Nguyen, Vijay Prakash Dwivedi, Gunther Gust
abstract: Relational deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning end-to-end predictive models over relational databases by representing them as temporal heterogeneous graphs. Recent advances based on graph neural networks and Transformers have achieved strong performance across diverse domains. However, the effectiveness of simpler relational baselines remains underexplored, making it difficult to assess how much architectural complexity is needed to achieve strong predictive performance. Motivated by the observation that predictive signals arise from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, we revisit how effectively these signals can be exploited using simple propagation methods. We adapt fixed low-pass feature propagation to relational entity graphs and train an MLP for prediction. The resulting predictions are further refined using Correct-and-Smooth, a graph-based label propagation algorithm that incorporates historical labels over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. Across classification and regression tasks on RelBench, an MLP trained on neighborhood-filtered features outperforms one using only target-entity features on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of the performance of heterogeneous GNNs. Correct-and-Smooth provides further gains from historical labels, although applying it requires a separately constructed meta-graph because connections among target entities are not directly specified by the relational entity graph. Together, our studies revisit the effectiveness of established propagation methods as simple RDL baselines while identifying canonical meta-graph construction as a key challenge for effective label propagation.

infographic.key_insight: Simple propagation-based baselines—filtered features plus an MLP, then label smoothing—recover much of the performance of more complex relational deep learning models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For relational databases modeled as temporal heterogeneous graphs, this suggests strong practical value in low-complexity pipelines before adopting heavier GNN or Transformer architectures.
method: Apply fixed low-pass feature propagation on the relational entity graph to denoise and mix neighborhood information.
Train an MLP on the propagated features for the main prediction task.
Refine predictions with Correct-and-Smooth using a task-specific meta-graph that propagates historical labels among target entities.
infographic.evidence_signal: On RelBench classification and regression tasks, neighborhood-filtered features usually beat target-entity-only features and capture a substantial share of heterogeneous GNN performance.
infographic.watch_item: Correct-and-Smooth depends on a separately constructed meta-graph, so label propagation is not plug-and-play when target-entity connections are not explicitly given.
infographic.paper_title: Revisiting Simple Baselines for Relational Deep Learning

title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal, Jialin Zhang, Yilin Chen, Qiuyang Mang
abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.

infographic.key_insight: Automated research agents scale better when they periodically forget past search history and restart from the best solution, rather than accumulating ever more context.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For practical AI discovery systems, memory management is a scaling lever: resetting agent state can deliver more progress per compute than simply running longer or adding more parallel agents.
method: Run multiple LLM agents with scored verification and inter-agent communication.
Periodically discard each agent’s session and candidate history.
Restart from the best candidate found so far to unblock further search.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four tasks in heuristic programming, kernel optimization, and model training, the forgetting strategy improved results by up to 15% over parallel agents and up to 39% over a single agent.
infographic.watch_item: Aggressive state resets may drop useful context, so the restart frequency and what is preserved as the “best candidate” need careful tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting

title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
authors: Luka Todorovic, Kaushal Gianchandani, Sai Ravela
abstract: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

infographic.key_insight: PolyNets turn known physics into a training-free neural network: a continuous-time polynomial dynamics module plus a recurrent integrator that preserves the numerical scheme while running efficiently on hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical way to emulate PDE solvers with GPU-friendly throughput and scalable ensembles without paying the cost of model training, while retaining solver-like accuracy.
method: Encode governing equations as polynomial dynamics in a continuous-time neural representation
Use a simple recurrent network to implement discrete-time integration
Exploit known coefficients so the tensor graph can run training-free and parallelized
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 1D KdV equation, PolyNet matched CPU/GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta accuracy across grid resolutions, 10^6 time steps, up to 10^4 trajectories, and different initial amplitudes.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on known governing coefficients and preserving the chosen numerical scheme, so applicability may be limited when the physics is incomplete or strongly uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation

title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling
authors: Wei Chen, Yubing Wu, Zhou Xu, Haoyue Zhang, Delu Zeng, Jiahao Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory's own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen--Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared $100$-step schedule, HP-RLVR trains $1.21\times$, $1.46\times$, and $2.30\times$ faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, $43.2\%$ (4B) and $49.0\%$ (8B) of GRPO's gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.

infographic.key_insight: HP-RLVR assigns token-level credit from a single rollout by comparing a model’s present-token view with a hindsight view of the realized future, avoiding group sampling while keeping reward signal even on failed attempts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scalable RLVR training, this offers a lower-rollout, no-critic alternative that can improve throughput and preserve usable gradients when many sampled attempts would otherwise collapse to the same terminal reward.
method: Single-rollout RLVR with token-level weighting from hindsight context
Compute a normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence between causal and hindsight token views
Use the divergence to weight reward relative to a historical baseline, with no reference solution or learned critic
infographic.evidence_signal: On paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared 100-step schedule, HP-RLVR was 1.21×, 1.46×, and 2.30× faster than GRPO on math, code generation, and ALFWorld using one-eighth the rollouts per prompt, with comparable overall accuracy and zero gradient records absent in HP-RLVR.
infographic.watch_item: The method depends on the generating policy snapshot and hindsight verifier feedback, so implementation quality and stability of the hindsight weighting may be sensitive to verifier design and task type.
infographic.paper_title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling

title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
authors: Daman Arora, Xuecheng Liu, Himanshu Gaurav Singh, Fahim Tajwar, Abitha Thankaraj, Ruslan Salakhutdinov
abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.

infographic.key_insight: GracefulRL trains language models to preserve normal task performance while learning to safely fall back when success looks unreliable, instead of encouraging risky guessing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is relevant for safety-critical software and automation, where a model should avoid producing harmful outputs or actions when confidence is low.
method: Use outcome-level reinforcement learning reward signals rather than fallback annotations.
Reshape optimization to make graceful failure stable under policy gradients.
Learn an explicit safe fallback policy that activates when acting is likely to be unreliable.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across a range of tasks and model scales, the abstract reports models that keep most task-solving ability while selectively falling back when success is out of reach.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract notes that naive policy-gradient training with intermediate fallback rewards is brittle, so careful optimization design is essential.
infographic.paper_title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully

title: When Does Task-Aware Imputation Matter? An Analysis of Robustness Under Train-Test Mismatch
authors: Maria V. Salvador, Ana F. Sequeira, Jaime S. Cardoso
abstract: Missing data is a pervasive challenge in machine learning, often degrading predictive performance and complicating model deployment. Most existing approaches treat imputation as a preprocessing step independent of the downstream task, a separation that becomes problematic under train-test mismatches in missingness mechanisms or rates. We introduce a unified framework that treats missing entries as variables in a task-conditioned optimization problem. We instantiate this framework in two settings: an amortized approach for scenarios with missing data at both training and test time, and a latent optimization approach for settings where only training data is incomplete. The evaluation is conducted on 98 tabular datasets, and robustness under train-test mismatches is assessed on 36 datasets. Results reveal that reconstruction error constitutes a poor proxy for predictive utility (Spearman rho approximately 0.16 to 0.32), and that task-aware imputation becomes critical in scenarios where classical methods fail to recover complete-data performance, achieving win rates of up to 80% in challenging train-test mismatch scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: Task-aware imputation—optimized for the downstream prediction task rather than reconstruction alone—can substantially improve robustness when missing-data patterns differ between training and test time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For deployed ML systems on tabular data, choosing imputation methods should be driven by predictive utility under expected missingness shifts, not by low reconstruction error.
method: Unified task-conditioned optimization treats missing entries as variables tied to the prediction objective.
Two instantiations: an amortized model for missing data at train and test time, and a latent optimization method for incomplete training data only.
Designed to handle train-test mismatches in missingness mechanisms or rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on 98 tabular datasets, with robustness under train-test mismatch tested on 36 datasets; reconstruction error showed weak correlation with predictive utility (Spearman rho ≈ 0.16–0.32), and task-aware methods achieved win rates up to 80% in hard mismatch settings.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits may depend on the availability of task labels and on the specific mismatch regime, so deployment should validate performance under the target missingness pattern.
infographic.paper_title: When Does Task-Aware Imputation Matter? An Analysis of Robustness Under Train-Test Mismatch

title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
authors: Delip Rao, Ahmed Muharram, Chris Callison-Burch
abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.

infographic.key_insight: LLM scientific claim verifiers can reach different verdicts depending on how they interpret an underspecified claim, so the interpretation should be recorded alongside the answer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI research agents and benchmark systems, exposing the agent’s claim interpretation improves traceability, makes disagreements diagnosable, and helps compare verdicts more fairly.
method: Defined a 9-field “Claim Card” to capture a verifier’s interpretation before evidence gathering, with fields marked stated, inferred, or default.
Ran a GPT-5.4 agent 5 times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims under three conditions: with a card, without a card, and with a frozen card.
Deliberately edited one card field (quantifier or support threshold) to test how interpretation changes affect verdicts and downstream tool use.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 900 runs, more than 40% of card fields were not stated; adding a card cost about 10% more tokens/time but did not measurably change agreement with expert labels, while targeted card edits changed verdicts on about one-third of claims (p < 0.001).
infographic.watch_item: A recorded interpretation may still be incomplete or inconsistently constructed, so benchmarks need a standard way to publish and compare both the claim label and the underlying interpretation.
infographic.paper_title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims

title: From Relevance to Validity: Zero-Shot Tool Selection via Functional and Contextual Validation
authors: Xiaoxuan Dong, Jin Zhang, Zichen Yuan, Yue Zhou, Zihao Rao, Dexu Yu
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face tasks from unseen domains and execution contexts, making zero-shot tool selection essential for identifying tools that can satisfy task requirements. Existing dominant methods mainly rely on relevance ranking, but semantic matching alone cannot ensure that a tool is functionally compatible or remains applicable in a new context. We preliminarily identify a \emph{transfer-validity gap}, where semantically relevant tools may still fail to satisfy functional or contextual requirements after transfer. To address this gap, we propose \methodname{}, a progressive validation framework that complements semantic relevance with endpoint-grounded functional compatibility and task-conditioned contextual evidence. Across cross-domain and cross-dataset transfer, \methodname{} consistently improves capability ranking, with larger gains under functional or contextual ambiguity. Ablation results further confirm the complementary contributions of functional and contextual validation.

infographic.key_insight: Zero-shot tool selection should validate not just semantic relevance, but whether a tool is functionally compatible and contextually applicable after transfer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM agents in unseen domains, this reduces failed tool calls by ranking tools on likely real-world usability rather than name or description similarity alone.
method: Stage 1: rank candidate tools by semantic relevance to the task.
Stage 2: check endpoint-grounded functional compatibility to verify the tool can actually satisfy the requirement.
Stage 3: use task-conditioned contextual evidence to confirm the tool remains valid in the new execution context.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports cross-domain and cross-dataset transfer evaluation, with consistent ranking improvements and especially larger gains under functional or contextual ambiguity.
infographic.watch_item: Functional and contextual validation may require reliable tool metadata, endpoint evidence, and context signals, which can be incomplete or noisy in practice.
infographic.paper_title: From Relevance to Validity: Zero-Shot Tool Selection via Functional and Contextual Validation

title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
authors: Qianru Meng, Xi Zhang, Konstantinos Papakostas, Congfeng Cao, Wenxiang Hu, Tianyi Lu
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.

infographic.key_insight: SwarmRSI evolves a swarm of scientific agents by using experimental feedback to both refine flawed hypotheses and recombine useful partial results, enabling recursive self-improvement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical loop for automating research workflows where multiple agent programs can share evidence, preserve useful components, and iteratively improve over time.
method: Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation: use other agents’ experimental feedback to revise hypotheses and implementations.
Complementary Swarm Recombination: merge retained hypotheses with useful program components across agents.
Recursive Swarm Evolution: close the loop by feeding new experimental evidence into the next research cycle.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art results on OpenProblems, NatureBench, and MLE-Bench Lite, plus improved performance on held-out tasks after accumulated research experience.
infographic.watch_item: A key concern is that partial program reuse and hypothesis mutation may propagate misleading components if experimental feedback is noisy or poorly attributed.
infographic.paper_title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm

title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
authors: Haofei Yu, Yixing Chen, Yining Zhao, Xuyan Ye, Yuxiang Liu, Zhigang Hua
abstract:
Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead. We propose 
ame, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, 
ame trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history. Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve. The policy still acts one step at a time at inference, with no overhead. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, $τ^2$-bench, and AppWorld), 
ame (1) achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets across simulated environments, while improving overall performance on both realistic applications; (2) delivers up to $1.9	imes$ and $2.0	imes$ higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO, respectively, on ScienceWorld; and (3) achieves these gains with a single policy backbone, without additional models, separate pretraining, or inference overhead. The codebase is available at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/CoPE.

infographic.key_insight: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting (CoPE) adds multi-step action forecasting to agent RL so the policy learns from intermediate trajectories, not just a terminal reward.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can improve sample efficiency and training stability for language agents in long-horizon tasks without adding inference-time cost or extra models.
method: Train on successful on-policy trajectories and supervise the policy to predict the next action sequence from prior histories.
Combine action forecasting with standard acting so both objectives shape a shared backbone during training.
Use a single policy backbone only; inference remains one-step action selection with no overhead.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, τ²-bench, and AppWorld), CoPE outperforms GRPO and predictive-auxiliary RL baselines, with up to 1.9× higher sample efficiency than ECHO and 2.0× higher than GRPO on ScienceWorld.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on successful on-policy trajectories and careful construction of multi-step action targets, which may be challenging in sparse-reward or noisy environments.
infographic.paper_title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents

title: The Accuracy Well: Nonmonotone Accuracy Dynamics at Vanishing Initialization
authors: Yaroslav Gusev, Eugene Golikov, Dmitry Yarotsky
abstract: We study classification dynamics under small initialization and identify a pronounced non-monotone behavior of accuracy that we call the accuracy well: accuracy rises rapidly early in training, subsequently drops, and only much later recovers. We observe this phenomenon in deep linear networks, fully connected ReLU networks on MNIST, deep convolutional networks on CIFAR-10, and controlled synthetic tasks, across different losses and optimizers and in both training and test accuracy. We propose a three-stage explanation in terms of target-driven organization, a degeneracy bottleneck, and subsequent recruitment and recovery. We develop a rigorous theory of these dynamics for shallow and deep linear networks, showing in particular that high accuracy can emerge while the predictor and the change in loss remain asymptotically vanishing, before continued optimization causes accuracy to deteriorate. For a simple synthetic classification task, we prove an extreme instance in which accuracy asymptotically rises to 100%, collapses to 0, and later recovers permanently to 100%. Our results show that classification accuracy can reveal aspects of learning dynamics that are not captured by the training loss alone.

infographic.key_insight: Small random initialization can create a pronounced nonmonotone "accuracy well," where accuracy improves early, drops sharply, and later recovers even as loss changes remain tiny.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This warns that training loss alone may miss important classification dynamics, so monitoring accuracy over time is crucial when diagnosing convergence and early stopping.
method: Observed the phenomenon across deep linear, ReLU, and convolutional networks.
Analyzed training under different losses and optimizers on synthetic and benchmark classification tasks.
Developed a rigorous theory for shallow and deep linear networks, including extreme collapse-and-recovery behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports empirical results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, deep linear networks, and controlled synthetic tasks, plus theoretical proofs for linear models and a synthetic case reaching 100% accuracy, then 0, then 100% again.
infographic.watch_item: The effect is tied to vanishing/small initialization and may be highly sensitive to training regime, so generalizing conclusions to standard initialization settings should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: The Accuracy Well: Nonmonotone Accuracy Dynamics at Vanishing Initialization

title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
authors: Yuyao Ge, Shenghua Liu, Peizhong Gao, Chendi Ge, Chenxu Liu, Yiwei Wang
abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

infographic.key_insight: Doc2Harness shows that for long-horizon coding agents, the quality of the surrounding harness can be as important as the model itself, and harness engineering is still very hard even for frontier LLMs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This benchmark gives practitioners a deterministic way to test whether a model can build robust agent scaffolding that works across isolated containers and realistic multi-step tool workflows.
method: Stage 1: a build model receives an interface-only contract skeleton plus a consolidated development document and constructs a candidate harness in an isolated container.
Stage 2: the frozen harness is executed in separate containers per test case and driven end-to-end by a scripted mock model.
Scoring uses four observable channels: model requests, files on disk, process exit code, and command output, with positive controls to prevent vacuous passes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 19 frontier models, 3 independent builds each, and 328 test cases, the top model reached 53.05% pass rate while the weakest was 27.44%, indicating substantial remaining failure modes.
infographic.watch_item: Because Stage 1 is build-time and Stage 2 is fully frozen, results may depend on how well the benchmark documents and isolates cross-cutting behavior that real harnesses often implement incrementally.
infographic.paper_title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
authors: Mohamed Bouadi, Nassim Bouarour, Aditya Tanna, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu
abstract: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.

infographic.key_insight: OrionMoE-Small improves tabular in-context learning by using dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts routing on top of a dual-axis Transformer, enabling adaptive computation without task-specific fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a compact, scalable alternative to dense tabular foundation models, especially for heterogeneous, small-context, and high-dimensional datasets.
method: Uses a dual-axis Transformer with distribution-aware feature representations.
Activates experts sparsely along the feature axis using routing informed by feature and dataset context.
Pretrains only on synthetic classification tasks from a structured causal prior, then predicts new tabular samples in-context.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive results across multiple tabular benchmarks, with particularly strong performance on small-context and high-dimensional datasets, plus improved behavior under class imbalance.
infographic.watch_item: Because the model is pretrained entirely on synthetic tasks, real-world generalization may depend on how well the synthetic causal prior matches target tabular domains.
infographic.paper_title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning

title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Yutong Wu, Yi-Xin Liu
abstract: Advances in polymer synthesis and computational modeling are expanding the block-copolymer architecture space accessible for phase-behavior design. Machine learning can accelerate this exploration, yet a common representation capable of learning across diverse chain topologies remains lacking. Here, we present a graph neural network (GNN) representation of acyclic AB multiblock architectures, tested by random-phase approximation (RPA) instability prediction. Each chain is represented as a graph, enabling a common model to learn across diverse topologies. This representation, which organizes RPA-related information, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks and demonstrates its potential for reuse across tasks through transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction. By effectively linking block-copolymer chain architecture to field-theoretic response, this graph representation not only reconstructs stability-limit curves but also provides a practical route for future self-consistent field theory exploration of ordered phase space across complex topologies.

infographic.key_insight: A graph neural network can encode diverse acyclic AB multiblock copolymer architectures in a single common representation and accurately predict RPA instability limits across topologies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reusable machine-learning tool for accelerating polymer phase-behavior design and exploring ordered-phase stability in complex block-copolymer architectures.
method: Represent each polymer chain as a graph rather than a fixed-length sequence.
Train a GNN on architecture-dependent RPA instability data to learn topology-to-response relationships.
Test extrapolation to larger block counts and transfer the learned representation to instability-wavenumber prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the model reconstructs stability-limit curves, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks, and transfers to a related prediction task.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well the training set covers chain topologies, so extrapolation to very different architectures or chemistry conditions should be validated carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits

title: ReAl: Refine neural operators via aligning dynamical flow
authors: Jing Xu, Zenglin Xu, Li Yi, Ruoxi Jiang, Yuan Qi
abstract: Neural partial differential equation (PDE) surrogates trained with mean squared error (MSE) can capture dominant dynamics but often lose high-frequency information and fine-scale structures. Generative models (e.g., Flow Matching) can capture the distribution of fine-scale details, yet stochastic errors may accumulate during autoregressive rollouts and compromise long-term stability. To address these limitations, we introduce Refine and Align(ReAl), a model-agnostic plug-in that augments pretrained PDE surrogates to improve the reconstruction of high-frequency structures associated with complex physical phenomena. In the refinement stage, a conditional flow-matching model learns the residual distribution around the deterministic base prediction, recovering missing fine-scale structures while retaining the dominant dynamics. In the alignment stage, to mitigate the generative discrepancies amplified in the autoregressive rollout, particularly in chaotic systems, we generate multiple trajectories from the same input and reinforce the refiner with trajectory-level rewards, thereby achieving long-horizon dynamical alignment. Experiments across diverse surrogate architectures and PDE tasks demonstrate that ReAl consistently improves high-frequency fidelity, forecasting accuracy, and long-horizon stability.

infographic.key_insight: ReAl is a model-agnostic plug-in that refines pretrained neural PDE surrogates by learning high-frequency residuals and aligning rollouts for long-horizon stability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It improves surrogate fidelity for simulations where fine-scale structures and stable autoregressive forecasts are critical, without requiring a new base PDE model.
method: Refinement: a conditional flow-matching model learns the residual distribution around the deterministic base prediction.
Alignment: multiple trajectories are sampled from the same input and used to reinforce the refiner with trajectory-level rewards.
Outcome: the plug-in reconstructs missing fine-scale details while reducing rollout drift in chaotic dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments across diverse surrogate architectures and PDE tasks, showing consistent gains in high-frequency fidelity, forecasting accuracy, and long-horizon stability.
infographic.watch_item: Trajectory-level alignment may increase training and sampling cost, and performance could depend on the quality of the pretrained base surrogate and reward design.
infographic.paper_title: ReAl: Refine neural operators via aligning dynamical flow

title: Lifted State Policy Optimization: Internalizing Self-Correction through Transition Geometry
authors: Ren Zhuang, Ben Wang, Shuifa Sun
abstract: Preference optimization ranks final answers and trajectory RL maximizes aggregate returns, yet neither credits the local change that turns a flawed reasoning state into a better one. We introduce Lifted State Policy Optimization (LSPO), which establishes this finite, cost-adjusted transition as the primary unit of learning. Each textual answer is augmented with a learned continuous coordinate, forming a lifted state that an energy function evaluates and orders. A shaped reward drives energy descent net of edit and step costs, and an internalization loss absorbs selected low-energy answers into the direct generator. On Qwen3.5-27B, the resulting single-pass policy reaches 71.8% aggregate accuracy across mathematics, science, code, and logic benchmarks, matching test-time reflection at 71.9% with 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens. The pattern holds across dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, and matched controls confirm that transition credit and the lifted coordinate each contribute, as does answer internalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo.

infographic.key_insight: LSPO learns from the quality of reasoning transitions themselves by lifting each answer into a continuous state and optimizing energy descent through self-correction steps, rather than only scoring final outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables single-pass generation to approach test-time reflection performance while cutting latency and token use, making it attractive for production LLM systems that need stronger reasoning efficiency.
method: Augment each textual answer with a learned continuous coordinate to form a lifted state.
Use an energy function plus shaped reward to favor low-energy transitions after accounting for edit and step costs.
Internalize selected low-energy answers into the base generator to reduce reliance on reflection at inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Qwen3.5-27B, LSPO achieved 71.8% aggregate accuracy across math, science, code, and logic benchmarks, nearly matching test-time reflection at 71.9% while using 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds learned transition geometry and cost shaping, so performance may depend on stable energy calibration and careful tuning of edit-step costs across backbones and tasks.
infographic.paper_title: Lifted State Policy Optimization: Internalizing Self-Correction through Transition Geometry

title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
authors: Woobin Park, Jaeyeon Kim, Yilun Du, Sitan Chen, Bohyung Han
abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.

infographic.key_insight: A simple reconstruction pretraining stage can make one-step generative models much easier to train, removing much of the difficulty of later distributional optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Priming Models offer a lower-compute path to high-quality one-step generation, improving the training-compute versus sample-quality tradeoff for image and world-model generation.
method: Train first with a reconstruction objective, such as pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level.
Then fine-tune in feature space with distributional post-training.
Use this two-stage setup to prime the model before one-step generation training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, the method improves the training-compute/quality Pareto frontier and reaches FID 1.19 on ImageNet 256×256 with about one-tenth the training compute of comparable prior one-step methods.
infographic.watch_item: Results may depend on careful design of the priming reconstruction task and on whether the downstream feature-space post-training transfers well across domains.
infographic.paper_title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
